loText: Describe how the shape of the distribution of PITs can be used as an indicator of the quality of a VaR model.
question: Iercosan et al. pooled the PITs of hundreds of US bank subportfolios, each with a one-day 99% regulatory VaR model, into a single histogram. The histogram was humped across the middle deciles but also showed visible spikes in the 0.0–0.1 and 0.9–1.0 bins. Which interpretation is most consistent with this shape?

options.A: The models are uniformly conservative: the forecast distributions are too wide everywhere, including the tails.
options.B: The models are conservative in the body of the distribution, but their tails are thinner than realised P&L requires, so extreme outcomes are understated.
options.C: The models are aggressive in the body but conservative in the tails, so the 99% VaR overstates extreme losses.
options.D: The shape reflects serial dependence of the PITs rather than any miscalibration of the forecast distribution.

solution:
**Step 1 – Read the body**

A hump across the middle deciles: outcomes cluster near the centre of the forecasts, so in the body the forecasts are too wide (conservative).

**Step 2 – Read the ends**

Spikes at both ends: extreme outcomes land beyond the forecast tails more often than predicted, so the tails are too thin.

⇒ Conservative in the body, but tails thinner than realised P&L requires.

**Interpretation**

This is exactly GARP’s finding for subportfolio PITs: models are “fairly conservative in the body” while “the tails of these risk models are thinner than is required by the realizations of P&L”. It also matches the moment results: models overstate variance and understate kurtosis.

loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
question: A validator wants to test whether a desk’s daily PITs are independent over time, following the approach described by Berkowitz (2001). Which procedure is correct?

options.A: Apply the Anderson-Darling test to the PITs, because it weights the tails where clustered losses show up.
options.B: Transform each PIT into a standard normal value with the inverse normal CDF, then test the transformed series for dependence, for example by regressing it on its own lag and on lagged P&L.
options.C: Count the exceedances of the 99% VaR and apply Kupiec’s proportion of failures test to the count.
options.D: Regress the raw PITs directly on their lags, because their \[0,1\] support makes the normal transformation unnecessary.

solution:
**Step 1 – Why transform**

PITs live on the bounded interval \[0,1\]. Berkowitz notes it is easier to test independence outside that range, so each PIT is mapped to a standard normal value, $\Phi^{-1}(p_{t})$ (e.g. 0.046 becomes −1.69), to “avoid problems of inference due to bounded support”.

**Step 2 – Then test dependence**

The transformed series is tested with log-likelihood methods; GARP regresses it on its lag and on lagged P&L. Significant coeﬀicients mean the forecasts ignore information already available.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

Uniformity tests (KS, AD, CvM) and independence tests are separate steps; together they check i.i.d. uniformity, the PIT version of conditional coverage.

loText: Describe backtesting using PITs, and compare the various goodness-of-fit tests that can be used to evaluate the distribution of PITs: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the Anderson-Darling test, and the Cramér-von Mises test.
question: In Iercosan et al.’s study of 597 US bank subportfolios, the share whose PITs passed (did not reject) each uniformity test at the 1% level was about 21% for Kolmogorov-Smirnov, 11% for Anderson-Darling and 21% for Cramér-von Mises, against 67% passing Kupiec’s unconditional coverage test. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: Because the most tail-sensitive test rejected the most subportfolios, the models’ main weakness lies in the centre of the forecast distribution.
options.B: The models perform better on exceedance tests than on tests of the whole distribution, and Anderson-Darling, which weights the tails, has the most power to detect the misspecification.
options.C: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises tests are the more reliable, because they agree with each other and reject fewer models.
options.D: The PIT tests must be wrong, because a model that passes Kupiec’s test has a correctly specified forecast distribution.

solution:
**Step 1 – Exceedance tests vs distribution tests**

67% pass Kupiec, but only 11% to 21% pass the PIT uniformity tests.

⇒ The models do better at the single VaR percentile than across the whole distribution.

**Step 2 – Rank the tests**

AD rejects the most (only 11% pass). GARP: “as the power of the test increases, we are able to find fewer subportfolios which exhibit the desired properties”.

⇒ AD, the tail-weighted test, is the most powerful here.

**Interpretation**

Passing an exceedance test is weak evidence that the whole forecast distribution is right; PIT tests, especially AD, reveal the tail misspecification the counts miss.

Both banks lend to identical borrowers, and all borrowers were rated at the start of the year when economic conditions were benign. During the year the country enters a severe recession. Which of the following is the most likely observation about rating changes at year‑end?

options.A: Bank A’s ratings show substantially more downgrades than Bank B’s, because TTC ratings react most quickly to the recession.
options.B: Bank B’s ratings show substantially more downgrades than Bank A’s, because PIT ratings reflect current conditions while TTC ratings are robust to short‑term changes.
options.C: Both banks’ ratings show the same downgrades, because the borrowers and their fundamentals are identical.
options.D: Bank A’s ratings show more downgrades than Bank B’s, because TTC ratings look ahead across a full cycle and anticipate the recession.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. TTC ratings have a long‑term orientation covering at least one business cycle, so they are robust to short‑term changes and updated less frequently.
2. PIT ratings focus on the current, short‑term condition of the borrower (usually within one year), are more volatile and are updated promptly as new information arrives.
3. A severe recession is a short‑term shock to current conditions, so Bank B’s PIT ratings migrate down sharply while Bank A’s TTC ratings change little.

**REBUILT** — Original stem was ambiguous about whether a 2009‑2024 benign‑period migration matrix is TTC or PIT and had a 2023/2025 typo; rebuilt as a self‑contained TTC vs PIT comparison in a severe recession.

loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
question: Which of the following best characterizes a through‑the‑cycle (TTC) credit rating approach when compared to a point‑in‑time (PIT) approach?

options.A: TTC assessments react swiftly to short‑term economic fluctuations and are frequently updated to reflect the current credit condition of the borrower.
options.B: PIT ratings take a long‑term perspective, often encompassing a full business cycle, and aim to remain stable against economic ups and downs.
options.C: TTC ratings have a long‑term view and tend to be less sensitive to short‑term economic conditions than PIT ratings.
options.D: Both TTC and PIT ratings prioritize near‑term economic indicators and are subject to frequent revisions.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. TTC: long‑term orientation covering at least one business cycle, robust to short‑term changes, less frequent updates.
2. PIT: current and short‑term condition (about one year or less), more volatile, updated promptly.
3. Only C attributes the long‑term, less sensitive profile to TTC.

loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
question: For an investor with a short‑term trading strategy, which of the following credit rating systems would likely be more informative?

options.A: A TTC rating system that provides a long‑term view of credit risk based on a borrower’s performance across business cycles.
options.B: A PIT rating system that reflects the borrower’s current and near‑term credit risk and adjusts quickly to market and economic changes.
options.C: A credit rating system that remains static over time, providing consistency rather than responsiveness.
options.D: A hybrid system that combines TTC and PIT elements and is updated semi‑annually.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. Short horizon means current credit condition matters most.
2. PIT ratings capture current, short‑term condition and are updated promptly.
3. So the PIT system (B) is more informative.

loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the frequency of updates in credit rating systems?

options.A: TTC rating systems are updated more frequently than PIT systems to give a timely reflection of economic conditions.
options.B: PIT rating systems are typically updated less frequently, coinciding with significant shifts in the business cycle.
options.C: PIT rating systems are updated more frequently than TTC systems to incorporate current conditions and short‑term trends.
options.D: Both TTC and PIT systems are updated on a fixed annual schedule regardless of economic or borrower changes.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. TTC ratings are robust to short‑term changes and subject to less frequent updates.
2. PIT ratings are updated in a timely manner to reflect new information on the borrower.
3. Hence PIT is updated more often than TTC.

loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
question: MatrixBank uses a through‑the‑cycle (TTC) rating system to evaluate borrower creditworthiness. Due to recent economic volatility, it is considering supplementing it with a point‑in‑time (PIT) system, and the board is divided. The CRO will compare the two systems using two borrowers: Firm A, a long‑standing client with cyclically stable revenues, and Firm B, a tech startup with rapid growth but facing current market uncertainty. Which of the following BEST reflects the distinctive features and appropriate application of TTC and PIT systems?

options.A: TTC is more suitable for Firm B, giving a stable outlook that mitigates the startup’s uncertain growth; PIT best serves Firm A by frequently updating its rating in line with stable market conditions.
options.B: PIT is preferred for both firms because real‑time risk assessment is critical for all borrowers, regardless of revenue stability.
options.C: TTC should be applied to Firm A, given its stable long‑term revenue and a consistent rating less affected by market fluctuations; PIT is ideal for Firm B, reflecting the immediate environment affecting the startup’s rapidly changing situation.
options.D: MatrixBank should use TTC exclusively for all clients because its long‑term stability suits a conservative strategy, despite the recent volatility.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. TTC: long‑term, cycle‑spanning, stable, less frequently updated; fits a borrower with stable long‑run fundamentals (Firm A).
2. PIT: current, short‑term, volatile, promptly updated; fits a borrower whose condition is changing quickly (Firm B).
3. C matches each system to the borrower it suits.

loText: Describe the approaches used and the challenges faced in modeling derivatives risk.
question: A bank that has long applied backtested market‑risk VaR models is extending its framework to measure counterparty risk using potential future exposure (PFE). A senior risk officer asks the model validation team how PFE modeling differs from VaR. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

options.A: PFE is the credit risk analogue of VaR but looks years ahead rather than a few days, which adds complexity and makes the models prone to misinterpretation and misuse.
options.B: PFE is easier to backtest than VaR because it is measured over a single day.
options.C: PFE measures the loss from a fall in value of the portfolio, whereas VaR measures only gains on the portfolio.
options.D: PFE avoids correlation and dependency problems because it is derived from the counterparty’s default probability alone.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. PFE is the counterparty risk equivalent of VaR, measuring credit exposure from gains.
2. Its horizon is many years versus a short VaR horizon (a few days), so historical simulation and backtesting are harder.
3. Dependency between risk factors, including wrong‑way risk, must also be modeled, adding complexity.

loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
question: A credit risk manager at a German bank is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts on the rating philosophies used across the bank. Its internal rating system for the short-term trade finance book is point-in-time (PIT), its economic capital model currently uses through-the-cycle (TTC) PDs, and its bond portfolio relies on agency ratings. Which of the following statements is correct for the manager to make?

options.A: Because TTC ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, they are the more volatile of the two philosophies and the more procyclical.
options.B: TTC assessments are mainly employed in banks’ internal systems for short-term loans, while PIT assessments are primarily of interest for the major credit rating agencies.
options.C: Research shows that PIT assessments have unambiguously higher predictive power than TTC assessments, so the bank should use PIT PDs for every purpose, including economic capital.
options.D: Switching the economic capital model from TTC to PIT PDs would make capital more volatile and procyclical, because a borrower is less likely to keep the same rating under a PIT approach.

solution:
**Step 1 – Which philosophy is volatile**

Doumpos: PIT ratings “are more volatile, and they are updated in a timely manner”; TTC assessments “are robust to short-term changes and they are subject to less frequent updates”.

**Step 2 – What that does to economic capital**

Crouhy, Galai and Mark: “The probability of a firm’s staying in the same rating when it is assessed using a PIT approach is smaller than when it is assessed using a TTC approach. ⇒ D is correct. The bank’s current split (PIT for short-term trade finance, TTC for economic capital) is exactly Crouhy’ […]

loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
question: Which of the following statements regarding risk assessment is most accurate?

options.A: Risk and control self‑assessments (RCSAs) are a good mixture of qualitative and quantitative aspects.
options.B: The main purpose of risk assessment is to prioritize risk management and risk mitigation responses.
options.C: When backtesting the results of risk assessment against past incident experience, there is a tendency to overestimate the likelihood of an operational risk event.
options.D: When backtesting the results of risk assessment against past incident experience, there is a tendency to underestimate the impact of an operational risk event.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. RCSAs are qualitative and largely judgment based, so A is wrong.
2. Backtesting against past incidents shows participants underestimate likelihood and overestimate impact, so C and D are reversed.
3. The main purpose of risk assessment is to prioritize risk management and mitigation responses: B.

loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
question: The board of a fast‑growing US‑based bank is reviewing a regulatory report that identified deficiencies in the bank’s model validation process. The CRO consults Federal Reserve guidance to improve validation. Which of the following recommendations is appropriate?

options.A: Require internal auditors who assess the bank’s model risk management framework to also validate and backtest the models
options.B: Begin monitoring each model’s performance only after its backtest has been successfully completed
options.C: Ensure third‑party vendor models are implemented under the assumptions initially provided by the vendor
options.D: Establish a continuous process of model risk management and validation rather than reviews at specific points in time

solution:
**Step by step**

1. Validation should be ongoing, reflecting changes in products, markets and model use; periodic‑only reviews lag.
2. A fails independence: auditors assessing the framework should not also validate the models.
3. B is wrong because monitoring begins once the model is put into use; C is wrong because vendor models must be validated for the bank’s own use and may need customization.

loText: Explain challenges that arise when using RAROC for performance measurement, including choosing a time horizon, measuring default probability, and choosing a confidence level.
question: Which of the following statements regarding the choice of default probability approaches in computing economic capital is correct?

options.A: A through‑the‑cycle (TTC) approach should be used to price financial instruments with credit risk exposure.
options.B: A point‑in‑time (PIT) approach is more commonly used for computations involving profitability and strategic decisions.
options.C: A TTC approach is more likely to result in a lower volatility of capital compared to the PIT approach.
options.D: A firm’s rating will not change when analyzed under the PIT approach versus the TTC approach.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. PIT PDs respond to current conditions, so a firm’s rating is more likely to change under PIT than TTC.
2. Hence TTC gives lower volatility of economic capital.
3. PIT suits pricing credit‑risk instruments and near‑term expected loss; TTC suits economic capital, current profitability and strategic decisions.

loText: Within the economic capital implementation framework, describe the challenges that appear in: - Defining and calculating risk measures - Risk aggregation - Validation of models - Dependency modeling in credit risk - Evaluating counterparty credit risk - Assessing interest rate risk in the banking book
question: A bank uses point‑in‑time (PIT) default probabilities for day‑to‑day credit portfolio management, but through‑the‑cycle (TTC) default probabilities for its economic capital calculation. The economy is now entering a severe recession. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: PIT default probabilities will rise sharply, while TTC probabilities will change little, so TTC‑based economic capital understates near‑term default risk relative to a PIT view.
options.B: TTC default probabilities will rise sharply, while PIT probabilities will change little, so PIT‑based measures understate near‑term default risk.
options.C: PIT and TTC default probabilities must be identical because both use the same time horizon.
options.D: PIT default probabilities will fall in a recession because rating migrations are smoothed over the cycle.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. PIT PDs reflect current conditions, so they move up quickly as the cycle deteriorates.
2. TTC PDs are averaged across the cycle and are relatively stable, so they respond little to the downturn.
3. Hence EC built on TTC PDs does not reflect the elevated near‑term risk that PIT PDs show.
4. The BIS notes that even with the same default horizon, PIT PDs for day‑to‑day use and TTC estimates for EC can coexist ‑ they are different estimates.

**REBUILT** — Original stem never stated which approach the migration matrix used, so options were not answerable; rebuilt around the point‑in‑time vs through‑the‑cycle issue described in the BIS paper.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question:
A bank has three derivatives with a single counterparty, covered by an enforceable bilateral netting agreement (EUR million):

| Transaction | Principal | Current value |
|---|---|---|
| 2‑year interest rate swap | 1000 | 95 |
| 5‑year foreign exchange forward | 1000 | ‑35 |
| 8‑month option on a stock | 700 | 80 |

What is the net replacement ratio (NRR) under the 1995 Amendment?
solution:
**Step by step**

1. NRR = current exposure with netting / current exposure without netting = max$(\sum V_{i}, 0)/ \sum\text{max}(V_{i}, 0)$.
2. With netting: 95 − 35 + 80 = 140 (positive, so no floor applies).
3. Without netting only positive values count: 95 + 0 + 80 = 175.
4. NRR = 140/175 = 0.80.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: A bank applying Basel I with the 1995 netting amendment has three derivatives with the same counterparty, covered by an enforceable bilateral netting agreement: (a) a seven‑year interest rate swap, notional \$400 million, current value ‑\$3 million; (b) a three‑year interest rate swap, notional \$170 million, current value +\$7 million; (c) a four‑month commodity derivative, notional \$80 million, current value +\$4 million. What is the net replacement ratio (NRR)?
solution:
**Step by step**

1. Current exposure with netting $= \text{max}(-3 + 7 + 4, 0) = 8$.
2. Current exposure without netting = 0 + 7 + 4 = 11 (the negative value is floored at zero).
3. NRR = 8/11 = 0.727.

options.A: Current exposure method
options.B: Original exposure method

options.D: Foundation internal ratings‑based approach

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: The 1995 Amendment to Basel I allowed reductions in credit equivalent amounts when enforceable bilateral netting agreements were in place. Shortly afterwards the 1996 Amendment added capital for market risk. Which of the following statements about the 1996 Amendment is TRUE?

options.A: It introduced the third pillar, which was praised for giving supervisors a consistent rule‑enforcing playbook
options.B: Conditional on meeting several criteria, including daily backtesting, banks could now employ their own internal value at risk (VaR) model to determine capital requirements for market risk
options.C: To reduce regulatory arbitrage, it removed all internal approaches so that only standardized approaches could be applied to credit, market, and operational risk
options.D: It removed Tier 2 capital so that only Tier 1 capital remained, with Tier 1 split into common equity and non‑common equity

solution:
**Step by step**

1. The 1996 Amendment offered a standardized measurement method and an internal model‑based approach for market risk.
2. Under the internal approach a bank uses its own 10‑day 99% VaR, multiplied by a factor of at least 3, provided qualitative criteria are met and the one‑day 99% VaR is backtested over the previous 250 days.
3. The three pillars came with Basel II; operational risk capital was also a Basel II innovation.
4. The Amendment added Tier 3 capital for market risk; it did not remove Tier 2. So only B is true.

question:
A bank has the following derivatives with two counterparties, each covered by an enforceable bilateral netting agreement (\$ millions):

| Counterparty | Derivative | Maturity (yrs) | Notional | Market value | Add‑on factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Interest rate | 2 | 100 | 20 | 0.5% |
| 1 | Interest rate | 3 | 100 | 0 | 0.5% |
| 1 | Wheat | 2 | 200 | ‑5 | 5% |
| 2 | Equity | 6 | 100 | 0 | 10% |
| 2 | Foreign exchange | 0.5 | 300 | ‑10 | 10% |

Using the 1995 Amendment, CEA $= \sum_{i} \text{max}(\sum_{j} V_{ij}, 0)+\sum_{j} L_{j}[0.4D_{j}+0.6D_{j}\times\text{NRR}]$, what is the total credit equivalent amount?

options.B: \$43.35 million
options.C: \$58.35 million
options.D: \$66.00 million

solution:
**Key correction:** Source key (BT answers) said A (\$33.05 million, NRR 0.25); correct is C because netting applies within each counterparty only: the ‑10 on counterparty 2 cannot offset the positive exposure to counterparty 1.

**Step by step**

1. Net exposure by counterparty: CP1 $= \text{max}(20 + 0 - 5, 0) = 15$; CP2 $= \text{max}(0 - 10, 0) = 0$. Total = 15.
2. Gross exposure (positive values only) = 20, so NRR = 15/20 = 0.75.
3. Add‑ons (notional x factor): 0.5 + 0.5 + 10 + 10 + 30 = 51.
4. Add‑on after netting = 51 × (0.4 + 0.6 × 0.75) = 51 × 0.85 = 43.35.
5. CEA = 15 + 43.35 = 58.35.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: The 1996 Amendment to the 1988 Basel Accord (implemented in 1998) required capital for the market risks of trading activities and distinguishes between the banking book and the trading book. About these books, each of the following is true EXCEPT, which is false?

options.A: The trading book consists of instruments that are actively traded and marked to market daily; the banking book consists primarily of loans that are held to maturity and not marked to market daily
options.B: The 1996 Amendment introduced a capital charge for the market risk associated with all items in the trading book
options.C: Under the 1996 Amendment, the credit risk capital charge in the 1988 Accord continued to apply to all on‑balance‑sheet and off‑balance‑sheet items in the trading and banking book, except positions in the trading book that consisted of (i) debt and equity traded securities and/or (ii) positions in commodities and foreign exchange
options.D: The 1996 Amendment eliminated the standardized measurement method for the calculation of market risk and abolished the distinction between the banking and trading books due to widespread regulatory arbitrage between the two

solution:
**Step by step**

1. The 1996 Amendment required fair‑value (mark‑to‑market) accounting for trading book positions held for trading; the banking book (loans, some debt securities held for investment) is not marked to market. A is true.
2. It added a market risk capital charge on trading book items, using the standardized measurement method or the internal model‑based approach. B is true.
3. Credit risk capital under Basel I continued to apply, except to trading book debt/equity securities and FX/commodity positions, which fall under the market risk charge. C is true.
4. The Amendment created two methods (standardized and internal model‑based) and relied on the banking/trading book distinction; it did not eliminate either. D is false.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: About the calculation of market risk under the 1996 Amendment, each of the following is true EXCEPT, which is false?

options.A: The standardized approach assigns capital separately to each of debt securities, equity securities, foreign exchange risk, commodities risk, and options; but no account is taken for correlations between different types of instruments
options.B: If a bank elects to use the historical simulation (HS) approach to calculating its value‑at‑risk (VaR), then a backtest is not required because an HS is effectively already a backtest
options.C: In the internal model‑based approach (IMA), the value‑at‑risk (VaR) measure used is calculated with a 10‑day time horizon and a 99.0% confidence level
options.D: Most large banks preferred to use the internal model‑based approach because it better reflected the benefits of diversification and led to lower capital requirements

solution:
**Step by step**

1. Test each statement against the 1996 Amendment.
2. A: the standardized method charges each category separately and ignores correlations ‑ true.
3. B: the amendment requires daily backtesting of the one‑day 99% VaR over the most recent 250 days for each model, regardless of how VaR is computed ‑ so the claim is false.
4. C: IMA uses a 10‑day, 99% VaR ‑ true.
5. D: IMA reflects diversification, gives lower capital, and was preferred by banks with material trading books ‑true.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: Saugatuck National Bank uses the internal model‑based approach to set market risk capital as prescribed by the 1996 Amendment to the 1988 Basel Accord. The bank has backtested its 99% one‑day VaRs against the actual losses over the last 250 trading days and recorded 11 exceptions. Based on these results, the multiplicative factor (m) should be set:

options.A: less than 3.
options.B: equal to 3.
options.C: between 3.1 and 3.9.
options.D: equal to 4.

solution:
**Step by step**

1. Backtest window: 250 days; exceptions = 11.
2. Rule (GARP): five or fewer exceptions in 250 days allow m = 3; more than five but fewer than ten can lead to a larger multiplier at the supervisor’s discretion; 10 or more require m = 4.
3. 11 >= 10, so m = 4.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: Under the 1996 Amendment to Basel I, for which of the following trading book positions is a capital charge for specific risk required?

options.A: Only fixed income positions measured under the standardized method
options.B: Only equity positions measured under the standardized method
options.C: Only positions measured under the internal model‑based approach
options.D: Fixed income and equity positions under the standardized method, and positions under the internal model‑based approach

solution:
**Step by step**

1. Under both approaches, capital is computed separately for specific risk (SR) and general market risk (MR) in each of the five categories.
2. Standardized method: SR charges apply to fixed income, equity and derivatives, so A and B are each incomplete.
3. Internal models: SR may be modelled but the multiplier is 4 rather than 3 and SR capital cannot be less than half of the standardized SR capital.
4. Hence SR capital is required in all cases: D.

question:
A market risk analyst at a Canadian bank is calculating the bank’s Basel 2.5 market risk capital charge for the trading book. The bank computes one-day 99% figures by historical simulation and scales them to 10 days with the square-root-of-time rule. A large position was added to the book two days ago. Data (CAD million, one-day 99%):

- VaR on the previous day: 6.5; average VaR over the last 60 trading days: 1.6
- Stressed VaR on the previous day: 7.4; average stressed VaR over the last 60 trading days: 6.9
- Backtesting exceptions over the last 250 trading days: 4

The supervisor applies, to both terms, the multiplier that this backtesting result permits under the 1996 Amendment. Which of the following is closest to the market risk capital charge?

options.A: CAD 20.6 million
options.B: CAD 27.2 million
options.C: CAD 80.6 million
options.D: CAD 86.0 million

solution:
**Step 1 – Multiplier**

Four exceptions is in the green zone (four or fewer), so $m_{c} = m_{s} = 3$.

⇒ The backtest is clean; a multiplier of 4 is required only at 10 or more exceptions.

**Step 2 – VaR term (one-day)**

max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c}\text{VaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(6.5, 3 \times1.6) = \text{max}(6.5, 4.8) = 6.5$

⇒ After the position build-up, yesterday’s VaR exceeds three times the 60-day average, so the previous-day term binds.

**Step 3 – Stressed VaR term (one-day)**

max$(\text{SVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s}\text{SVaR}_{avg}) = \text{max}(7.4, 3 \times6.9) = \text{max}(7.4, 20.7) = 20.7$

⇒ Stressed VaR is stable, so the multiplied average binds as usual.

**Step 4 – Scale to 10 days and add**

MR$_{2.5} = (6.5 + 20.7) \times\sqrt{10} = 27.2 \times3.1623 = 86.01$
